question:
Patient note:
A 58-year-old man with a decade-long history of systolic left-ventricular dysfunction secondary to a remote anterior myocardial infarction (last documented ejection fraction 28 % on an outpatient echocardiogram four months ago, managed with carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, sacubitril/valsartan 49–51 mg twice daily, furosemide 40 mg each morning, and spironolactone 25 mg nightly) was brought to the emergency department by ambulance at 03:15 after abruptly vomiting several mouthfuls of bright-red fluid mixed with small clots while sitting upright in a recliner watching late-night television; he described a fleeting, burning epigastric sensation just before the retch but denied any black, sticky, foul-smelling stools and reported that his last bowel movement the previous afternoon was light-brown, formed, and looked entirely ordinary. Paramedics found him seated, pale, and sweating, with a radial pulse they estimated in the 130s; he refused IV access in the field, stating he “didn’t want needles in the living room,” and no crystalloids, antiemetics, or acid suppressive agents were started en route. He has never been told he has hepatitis, cirrhosis, or abnormal liver enzymes, drinks only a bottle of light beer on weekends, quit smoking fifteen years ago after a fifteen-pack-year exposure, and has no prior endoscopic evaluation. Other medical issues include stage 2 chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 1.2 mg/dL) and chronic knee osteoarthritis for which he intermittently takes over-the-counter naproxen 440 mg twice daily, most recently for the past week after mowing his lawn. His daily regimen notably excludes aspirin, clopidogrel, warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants, glucocorticoids, or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Family history reveals a father with coronary artery disease and a mother who died of breast cancer; no relatives have bleeding disorders. Review of systems obtained in the ambulance and expanded on arrival is negative for fever, chills, cough, hemoptysis, jaundice, pruritus, abdominal distention, ankle swelling beyond his chronic trace edema, or change in urinary output. He did note progressive fatigue over the previous two days that he attributed to summer heat but had been able to walk from his bedroom to the kitchen without needing to stop for breath—consistent with his usual New York Heart Association class II baseline. On arrival to triage—before insertion of any IV lines, administration of fluids, vasoactive medications, transfusion, or proton-pump inhibitor therapy—he sat hunched forward in a wheelchair clutching an emesis basin streaked with fresh blood, lips pale, skin cool and clammy, but still answering questions coherently in complete sentences. Manual vitals obtained with the cuff at heart level recorded a blood pressure of 82/48 mm Hg; simultaneous monitor waveform showed a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 133 beats per minute; respiratory rate was 24 per minute, oral temperature 36.7 °C, and oxygen saturation 96 % while breathing ambient air. Capillary refill exceeded four seconds; conjunctivae were markedly blanched, sclerae anicteric, and oropharynx contained thin streaks of bright-red fluid without coffee-ground debris. Jugular venous pulsation reached the angle of the mandible at 45°, bilateral lung bases revealed fine crackles that cleared with coughing, and there was a soft third heart sound consistent with his established cardiomyopathy but no new murmurs or pericardial rub. Peripheral pulses were rapid and thready, and 1+ pitting edema was noted at both ankles. The abdomen was scaphoid and soft; gentle palpation elicited mild tenderness in the epigastrium without guarding, rebound, palpable masses, or organ enlargement. Bowel sounds were brisk. Neurologic screening showed an alert, oriented individual with 5/5 strength in all extremities but slowed mentation when answering complex questions, likely from hypoperfusion. A single 16-gauge catheter was then placed in the right antecubital vein purely for diagnostic phlebotomy; at that very moment the patient had not yet received crystalloid resuscitation, vasopressors, opioids, antiemetics, acid suppressive therapy, or blood products. Initial laboratory results returned within twelve minutes: hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL, hematocrit 22 %, mean corpuscular volume 88 fL, platelet count 210 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 12.1 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 68 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL (slightly above his known baseline), sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, glucose 108 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.07. A 12-lead electrocardiogram printed concurrently revealed sinus tachycardia at 134 bpm with nonspecific ST-T changes unchanged from outpatient tracings. Upright portable chest radiography demonstrated cardiomegaly with mild pulmonary vascular congestion but no focal infiltrate or effusion, while a single-view abdominal radiograph displayed a nonspecific gas pattern without free intraperitoneal air. At this very early snapshot he remains nil per os on continuous cardiac and blood pressure monitoring, a type-and-screen is processing, and gastroenterology has been paged for urgent esophagogastroduodenoscopy to identify and control the presumed proximal source of his brisk hematemesis complicated by profound anemia and decompensated hemodynamics in the setting of chronic systolic heart disease.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score uses admission urea, sex-specific hemoglobin, systolic pressure, pulse, melena, syncope, hepatic disease, and heart failure.
- BUN 68 mg/dL corresponds to urea 68/2.8 = 24.3 mmol/L. This falls in the 10 to <25 mmol/L band = 4.
- Male hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL (<10) = 6.
- Systolic pressure 82 mm Hg (<90) = 3.
- Pulse 133/min (≥100) = 1.
- No melena = 0; no reported syncope = 0. Hematemesis is not a separate point item.
- No known hepatic disease = 0; established systolic heart failure with EF 28% = 2.
Total = 4 + 6 + 3 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 16.
Final answer: 16
